facts.fact_text: The applicant, together with another person, intended to organise demonstrations to draw attention to the situation of those having foreign currency loans.
The applicant, together with another person, intended to organise demonstrations to draw attention to alleged fraudulent banking policies.
The applicant, together with another person, intended to organise demonstrations to put pressure on decision-makers so that respect for the rule of law gains primacy over the interests of oligarchs.
On 8 December 2014 the applicant notified the Budapest police department of his intention to organise a demonstration.
The demonstration was scheduled for 19 December 2014 between 9 a.m. and 8 p.m.

The demonstration was planned to take place at nine venues: the headquarters of different banks, the Israeli embassy, the Kúria, the home of the chief executive officer (CEO) of the biggest commercial bank in Hungary, the home of the prime minister, and the Offices of the National Assembly.
The demonstration was planned to include a march between the different locations.
The organisers specified that it was expected that about thirty to one hundred persons would participate in the demonstration.
The organisers specified that it was expected that about twenty to fifty cars would participate in the demonstration.
On 9 December 2014 the Budapest police department banned the holding of the demonstration outside the Kúria building.
On 9 December 2014 the Budapest police department banned the holding of the demonstration outside the home of the prime minister.
On 9 December 2014 the Budapest police department banned the holding of the demonstration outside the home of the CEO of the biggest commercial bank in Hungary.
The Budapest police department's decision held that the demonstration outside the Kúria was prohibited under section 8(1) of Act no. III of 1989 on the right to assembly (the Assembly Act).
The Budapest police department's decision held that the demonstration at the home of the prime minister would constitute a direct threat to the inhabitants' right to private and family life.

The Budapest police department's decision held that the demonstration at the home of the CEO of the biggest commercial bank in Hungary would constitute a direct threat to the inhabitants' right to private and family life.

The Budapest police department's decision held that the demonstration at the homes of the prime minister and the CEO of the biggest commercial bank in Hungary would constitute a direct threat to the inhabitants' right to property.

The Budapest police department's decision held that the demonstration at the homes of the prime minister and the CEO of the biggest commercial bank in Hungary would constitute a direct threat to the inhabitants' right to move around freely.

The Budapest police department's decision held that the demonstration at the homes of the prime minister and the CEO of the biggest commercial bank in Hungary was prohibited under section 2(3) of Act no. III of 1989 on the right to assembly (the Assembly Act).

Section 2(1) of Act no. III of 1989 on the right to assembly (the Assembly Act), as in force at the material time, provided that exercising the right to assembly covers holding peaceful assembly events, marches and demonstrations, where the participants may freely express their opinions.

Section 2(3) of Act no. III of 1989 on the right to assembly (the Assembly Act), as in force at the material time, provided that exercising the right to assembly shall not result in committing a criminal offence or incitement to committing a criminal offence and shall not result in the violation of the rights and freedoms of others.

Section 8(1) of Act no. III of 1989 on the right to assembly (the Assembly Act), as in force at the material time, provided that if the holding of an event subject to prior notification seriously endangers the proper functioning of the representative bodies or courts, or results in a disproportionate hindrance of the circulation of traffic, the police may prohibit the holding of the event at the place or time indicated in the notification, within forty-eight hours of receipt of the notification by the authority.

The reasoning of the Budapest police department's decision stated that according to information received from the vice-president of the Kúria, the aim of the demonstration, namely 'putting pressure on decision-makers', was unconstitutional.

The reasoning of the Budapest police department's decision stated that the aim of the demonstration, namely 'putting pressure on decision-makers', was likely to endanger the independence and proper functioning of the judiciary.
The Budapest police department's decision held that the demonstration at the home of the prime minister would constitute a direct threat to the inhabitants' right to private and family life.

The Budapest police department's decision held that the demonstration at the home of the CEO of the biggest commercial bank in Hungary would constitute a direct threat to the inhabitants' right to private and family life.

The Budapest police department's decision held that the demonstration at the homes of the prime minister and the CEO of the biggest commercial bank in Hungary would constitute a direct threat to the inhabitants' right to property.

The Budapest police department's decision held that the demonstration at the homes of the prime minister and the CEO of the biggest commercial bank in Hungary would constitute a direct threat to the inhabitants' right to move around freely.

The Budapest police department's decision held that the demonstration at the homes of the prime minister and the CEO of the biggest commercial bank in Hungary would be likely to frighten the children attending the nearby school.

The Budapest police department's decision held that the demonstration at the homes of the prime minister and the CEO of the biggest commercial bank in Hungary would endanger the safety of the protected persons living in the premises.
The organisers amended the agenda of the demonstration, reducing the time spent outside the Kúria building to ten minutes.
The organisers amended the agenda of the demonstration, reducing the time spent at the prime minister's home to ten minutes.
The organisers agreed to use megaphones only at the Kúria building and the prime minister's home.
The organisers agreed to approach the Kúria building and the prime minister's home only on foot.
The organisers agreed to change the aim of the demonstration from 'putting pressure on decision-makers' to 'raising public awareness'.
The Constitutional Court of Hungary found that the Budapest Administrative and Labour Court paid no heed to the organisers' intention to reduce the length of the demonstration.

The Constitutional Court of Hungary found that the Budapest Administrative and Labour Court's decision did not consider the length of the demonstration and the fact that it had been reduced in the course of the reconciliation procedure.

The Constitutional Court of Hungary found that since the petitioner had the possibility to express his opinion at a number of stages of the demonstration, his right to freedom of assembly had not been disproportionally restricted.

The Constitutional Court of Hungary stated that in exceptional circumstances the conflict between fundamental rights could result in the most severe restriction, namely banning a demonstration, but that the mere fact that there is a conflict between fundamental rights is not a sufficient ground for banning a demonstration.

The Constitutional Court of Hungary stated that in cases of a conflict between fundamental rights, with the exception of when there is good reason to ban a demonstration, there should be a way for the police to negotiate with the organisers of a demonstration in order to strike a balance that enables the holding of a demonstration and the exercise of other concurring fundamental rights protected by the Fundamental Law of Hungary.
The Constitutional Court of Hungary observed that the conciliation procedure, of primordial importance in guaranteeing fundamental rights, became only formal in the present case.

The Constitutional Court of Hungary reiterated that the role of the conciliation procedure is to remove the legal obstacles from holding a planned demonstration and, in the event it is successful, to pave the way for the exercise of the right to freedom of assembly.

The Constitutional Court of Hungary observed that the legal system does not define the standards and procedures the police have to take into account when reconciling the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and other fundamental rights in cases of conflict.

The Constitutional Court of Hungary found that the underlying reason for the restrictive judicial practice manifested in the present case is the lack of legal guarantees foreseeing less restrictive measures and conditions other than banning demonstrations.

The Constitutional Court of Hungary stated that it is the obligation of the legislature to provide guidance for those applying the legislation to effectively fulfil their obligations under Article I of the Fundamental Law of Hungary in cases of conflicting fundamental rights.
